newsitem.title: GERMANY: German banks must probe Nazi past.
newsitem.headline: German banks must probe Nazi past.

text.p: A Jewish community leader called on Germany's powerful commercial banks on Thursday to follow the lead of their Swiss counterparts and adopt a new openness towards their history during the Nazi era.

Michel Friedman, an executive council member of Germany's Central Council of the Jews, said it was high time the banks revealed their role in the Nazi "Aryanisation" programme to strip Jews of their money and other assets.
"For more than five decades we've been waiting for the officials of the banks which worked, cooperated and collaborated during the Third Reich to speak," Friedman said.
"It's high time we opened the archives to get comprehensive information about how it was then... during the expropriation of Jewish assets carried out with the help of the banks."

After strong pressure from world Jewry, Swiss banks last month lifted the veil of secrecy that traditionally surrounds their transactions to publish lists of dormant accounts which could have belonged to Holocaust victims.

Friedman said German banking records were not directly comparable with the Swiss case, as accounts held by Jews in Germany would have been legal and public and the names of the account holders would have been known.

"This case is about winding up these accounts," he told German Radio. "It's interesting to know how this system of expropriation worked and perhaps also interesting to know which banks were eager and which were over-eager."

Deutsche Bank AG, Germany's largest bank, authorised an account of its activities under the Nazis which found that the bank profited from the sale of Jewish property but also revealed its links to the resistance against Hitler.

"Our archives are always open to researchers. This is not a new issue for us," bank spokesman Ronald Weichert said. "It's a continuing process for us to deal with this issue. We will follow up every lead if requests are made by former clients."

A chapter written by eminent British historian Harold James in the bank's official history, published in 1995 at its 125th anniversary, concludes that the bank through its role in Aryanisation "loaded a heavy moral burden on itself."
But James adds: "The bank was to a considerable extent steered by forces it could not control."

Dresdner Bank AG, Germany's second-largest bank, announced last month it had commissioned Dresden University to research its history during the Third Reich. The project will be supported by an international group of historians.

Friedman said some banks were gradually researching the subject of their role during the Nazi era but a switch to a completely open information policy was required and not just "a couple of pages in jubilee brochures".

He said it was important to study how dictatorships could strip people of their rights. "I believe this is an obligation which goes beyond the realms of yesterday and also brings us forward, so that such mistakes can't be repeated."
